profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review at a university-industry ML systems lab for a camera-ready journal extension of an earlier prototype study on edge-IoT estimation of indoor environmental quality. The team is reviewing a near-final evaluation design comparing two already-chosen implementations: a centralized MQTT plus GPU pipeline and a distributed MPI plus ARM pipeline running lightweight MLP estimators over temperature and illuminance signals derived from controlled IEQ experiments. The agenda is to decide whether the comparison protocol, benchmark package, deployment notes, and reporting tables are specified well enough to approve the study design without reopening the architecture choice itself. The expected outcome is approval with minor revisions, plus a short action list for what gets frozen now versus what the implementation team can still finalize during execution.

members.name: Dr. Elena Varga
members.expertise: TinyML benchmarking, experimental design for embedded inference, reproducible evaluation pipelines
members.background: Elena leads the lab's benchmarking methodology track and has spent the last several years turning ad hoc embedded ML demos into reusable benchmark suites for academic and industrial edge platforms.
members.private_state: She wants the design approved in this meeting so the student team can start packaging experiments for the journal extension, and she is quietly trying to avoid any review comments that would force them to rerun the whole benchmark under a new protocol.
hidden_assumptions: When a comparison claims the architectures see the 'same workload,' fairness comes from replaying the exact same pre-segmented event windows and timestamps into both systems from a fixed benchmark bundle.

The phrase 'pilot temperature and illuminance dataset' refers to the cleaned repository artifact named pilot_ieq_v3_curated, not the original recorder dumps, because that is the version used to produce the draft figures.

A design is 'ready for comparison' once benchmark definitions, result schemas, and acceptance checks are frozen; wiring details that do not alter nominal model inputs can be settled during implementation.
The reported 'power consumption' figure should use the lab's usual active-processing window on the compute boards only, excluding warm-up, sensor baseline draw, and idle coordination periods.

If the design note says the event families are spikes, square profiles, and sawteeth, everyone understands those as already-cut labeled windows rather than waveforms that still need to be detected online.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Distributed IoT execution, ARM-based edge deployment, sensor-network runtime instrumentation
members.background: Arjun designs deployable edge sensing systems for building and industrial environments and has repeatedly had benchmark-friendly prototypes fail to match field behavior once synchronization, buffering, and communication overhead were included.
members.private_state: He wants to protect the distributed method from being evaluated in a way that looks clean on paper but is disconnected from how MPI-style sensing nodes actually behave, while still sounding supportive of the paper timeline.
hidden_assumptions: When two architectures run the 'same workload,' each should process equivalent live sensor streams end to end, including local buffering, timestamp alignment, and communication effects, because those are part of the workload the architecture actually bears.

The phrase 'pilot temperature and illuminance dataset' naturally refers to the original logged time series captured in the chamber experiments, from which each node or pipeline forms windows during execution.
A design is only 'ready for comparison' when all measurement-affecting execution details are pinned down, especially synchronization source, logging boundaries, and where power is sampled.

The reported 'power consumption' number should represent the whole experimental run envelope for the architecture, including MPI coordination, waiting periods, message passing, and sensor polling, because that is what a deployment owner pays for.

If the event families are spikes, square profiles, and sawteeth, the important thing is that the runtime sees those patterns emerge from the stream and handles them online, not that identical pre-cut segments are replayed.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the centralized and distributed systems must be evaluated under the 'same workload.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means both architectures receive the same benchmark bundle of pre-segmented windows from the curated pilot_ieq_v3_curated package, with identical event slices and timing metadata replayed for strict comparability.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means both architectures experience equivalent end-to-end sensing conditions, where each pipeline ingests raw streams and performs its own buffering, segmentation, and communication handling during the run.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like ordinary fairness language in an ML systems review, and both believe they are defending comparability; the divergence hides in whether workload means benchmark inputs or full runtime burden, which is easy to leave implicit.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'pilot dataset' they are pointing to
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to reusing the 'temperature and illuminance pilot dataset' from the chamber experiments.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the curated repository artifact pilot_ieq_v3_curated, which contains normalized and labeled windows for the three event families used in the draft analysis.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the raw chamber logs exported from the acquisition gateway, with continuous temperature and lux time series that still include startup jitter and unsmoothed transitions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Inside the project, both artifacts are routinely called 'the pilot dataset,' and both genuinely originate from the same chamber experiment; because the naming overlap feels harmless and familiar, neither expects it to need disambiguation in a design review.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the evaluation design is 'ready for comparison' and can be signed off.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the design is ready once the benchmark package, metrics tables, and reporting rules are stable enough that implementation can proceed without changing the scientific claims structure.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the design should not be signed off until operational details that affect measured results are specified, including clock sync source, power logging start-stop boundaries, and message tracing points.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are talking about rigor and approval, so the conversation sounds aligned at the surface; in design reviews, 'ready' often ambiguously blends conceptual completeness with execution completeness, letting the stricter and looser thresholds coexist unnoticed.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both want the paper to preserve a clear 'power consumption' comparison, especially the distributed reduction result.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the number will be computed over active inference intervals on the GPU board or ARM nodes, excluding sensor idle draw, initialization, and coordination overhead so it matches the lab's previous benchmark tables.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the number should cover the entire architecture-level run from sensing start to result emission, including MPI waits, communication retries, and node-side polling overhead.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They both speak as if they are protecting the same headline power claim, and 'power consumption' normally sounds self-explanatory; the hidden mismatch is only in where the accounting boundary is drawn, which feels too mundane to restate unless someone anticipates a reporting dispute.

We do not need to reopen wiring details if they do not change the nominal model inputs or the reporting structure.
